concepts.name: WEO: Publishing Body, Frequency, and Institutional Mandate
key_dimensions: Published by IMF (not World Bank, OECD, or UN — a common UPSC trap)
Released twice annually: April (Spring Meetings) and October (Annual Meetings), with updates in January and July
Distinction from other IMF flagship reports: Global Financial Stability Report (GFSR) and Fiscal Monitor released simultaneously
Mandate: Analyze global economic developments, project growth, and assess risks — advisory, not binding

concepts.name: WEO Growth Projections: Methodology and Metrics Used
key_dimensions: Primary metric: Real GDP growth rate (not nominal GDP — a key distinction)
Use of Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) vs. Market Exchange Rate (MER) weightings and why WEO often uses PPP for global aggregates
Difference between 'Advanced Economies,' 'Emerging Market and Developing Economies (EMDEs),' and 'Low-Income Developing Countries (LIDCs)' classifications
Concept of 'output gap' and how WEO uses it to assess overheating or slack in an economy

concepts.name: WEO Country Classification System
key_dimensions: Three-tier classification: Advanced Economies (AEs), EMDEs, and LIDCs — criteria are not purely income-based (trap: unlike World Bank income classifications)
India's classification as an EMDE, not an Advanced Economy, despite being the 5th largest by MER
G7 vs. G20 country coverage in WEO projections and their overlap
Reclassification controversies: countries that have moved between categories (e.g., South Korea elevated to AE)

concepts.name: Concept of 'Synchronised Slowdown' and 'Decoupling' in WEO Analysis
key_dimensions: WEO's use of 'synchronised slowdown' to describe simultaneous deceleration across major economies (used prominently in 2019 WEO)
Distinction between synchronised slowdown and recession — threshold conditions
Decoupling debate: whether emerging markets (especially India/China) can sustain growth independent of AE slowdowns
Policy implications flagged by WEO: coordinated vs. unilateral fiscal/monetary responses

concepts.name: Global Recession Definition as Used in WEO
key_dimensions: IMF/WEO definition of global recession: global growth below 3% (NOT the technical 2-quarter negative growth rule used for individual countries — critical UPSC trap)
Historical global recessions identified by WEO: 1975, 1982, 1991, 2009, 2020
Distinction between 'per capita recession' (negative per capita GDP growth) vs. aggregate GDP recession
WEO's 'Scarring Effects' concept: permanent output loss post-recession vs. cyclical recovery

concepts.name: WEO's Treatment of Inflation: Concepts and Indicators
key_dimensions: WEO tracks CPI-based inflation as primary measure across countries (not WPI — trap for India-specific thinking)
Distinction between 'headline inflation' and 'core inflation' as used in WEO risk assessments
WEO's concept of 'Great Moderation' vs. post-2021 'Great Inflation' return — contextual framing
WEO warnings on 'de-anchoring of inflation expectations' and central bank credibility

concepts.name: Downside Risks and Upside Risks Framework in WEO
key_dimensions: WEO's standard risk taxonomy: geopolitical risks, financial market volatility, trade fragmentation, climate shocks
Concept of 'Fan Chart' or probability distribution used in WEO to show uncertainty around baseline forecasts
Distinction between 'tail risks' (low probability, high impact) vs. baseline risks in WEO parlance
Recent additions: 'Geoeconomic Fragmentation' as a structural downside risk (post-2022 WEO editions)

concepts.name: WEO Special Focus Themes and Analytical Chapters
key_dimensions: WEO typically contains 2 analytical chapters beyond projections (e.g., climate change, digitalization, debt sustainability)
Recent themes: Scarring from COVID-19 (2020-21), Inflation Surge (2022), AI and Productivity (2024) — UPSC loves recent themes
Distinction: WEO analytical chapters vs. World Development Report (World Bank) thematic focus — frequent confusion source
How WEO special themes influence G20 agenda and IMF Article IV consultations

concepts.name: India's Growth Projections in WEO: Patterns and Implications
key_dimensions: India consistently projected as 'fastest growing major economy' in multiple WEO editions (2022-2025) — factual anchor
WEO projections vs. RBI/CSO projections: understanding divergence and reasons (methodology, base year differences)
WEO flagging India-specific risks: inflation, current account deficit, financial sector vulnerabilities
India's weight in global GDP (PPP vs. MER) and how this affects global growth arithmetic in WEO

concepts.name: Concept of 'Potential Output' and 'Structural Reforms' in WEO
key_dimensions: WEO distinguishes cyclical growth (demand-driven) from structural/potential output growth (supply-side)
WEO's advocacy for structural reforms: labor markets, product markets, governance — standard WEO prescription
Concept of 'Total Factor Productivity (TFP)' as used in WEO growth accounting frameworks
WEO's position on 'premature deindustrialization' in developing economies — relevant for India's manufacturing push

concepts.name: WEO on Global Trade: Volumes, Fragmentation, and Protectionism
key_dimensions: WEO tracks global trade volume growth separately from GDP growth — historically trade grew ~2x GDP (now converging)
WEO's 'Geoeconomic Fragmentation' scenario: cost estimates of splitting world into two blocs (1-7% permanent GDP loss per WEO estimates)
Distinction between WEO trade analysis and WTO's World Trade Report — different mandates and metrics
WEO on 'Friendshoring' and 'Nearshoring' as emerging structural shifts in global supply chains

concepts.name: WEO and Fiscal Policy: Debt Sustainability and Consolidation
key_dimensions: WEO works alongside Fiscal Monitor but covers fiscal risks in its own chapters — overlap and distinction
WEO's concept of 'Fiscal Space': countries with room to stimulate vs. those requiring consolidation
Debt-to-GDP ratio thresholds discussed in WEO (not rigid rules, but ~90% for AEs flagged as risk zone — Reinhart-Rogoff debate)
WEO on 'Fiscal Multipliers': higher in recessions, lower in expansions — implication for austerity debates

concepts.name: WEO on Monetary Policy: Interest Rate Cycles and Central Bank Coordination
key_dimensions: WEO's tracking of 'Global Financial Conditions' and the role of US Fed rate decisions on EMDEs (spillover effects)
Concept of 'Taper Tantrum' (2013) and similar episodes discussed in WEO as EMDE vulnerability examples
WEO on 'Policy Rate' vs. 'Neutral Rate (r*)': implications of persistently low neutral rates for monetary policy space
WEO's position on central bank independence as a precondition for inflation credibility

concepts.name: WEO on Climate Change and Green Transition Costs
key_dimensions: WEO integrates climate risk into macroeconomic projections (post-2020 editions) — 'physical risks' vs. 'transition risks'
WEO's estimates on green transition investment needs: trillions annually for net-zero pathways
Distinction: WEO climate analysis vs. IPCC reports vs. World Bank Climate Change reports — mandate boundaries
WEO on carbon pricing as a macroeconomic instrument — revenue recycling and distributional effects

concepts.name: WEO on Inequality and Distributional Effects of Growth
key_dimensions: WEO's evolved mandate: from pure growth focus to inclusive growth (post-2015 SDG alignment)
WEO's use of Gini coefficient and income share data to track within-country inequality trends
WEO finding: globalization reduced between-country inequality but raised within-country inequality — key analytical insight
Distinction: WEO inequality analysis vs. UNDP Human Development Report and Oxfam Inequality Reports — different metrics and conclusions

concepts.name: WEO Forecast Accuracy and Revision Patterns
key_dimensions: WEO has historically over-estimated growth for EMDEs and under-estimated recessions (systematic optimism bias — documented)
Concept of 'Forecast Revision': downward vs. upward revision triggers and their signaling value for markets
WEO's own post-mortem: 2012 paper admitting fiscal multipliers were underestimated during eurozone austerity
UPSC angle: What does a WEO downgrade of India's growth mean vs. an upgrade — policy and credibility implications

concepts.name: WEO vs. Other Major Global Economic Reports: Comparative Framework
key_dimensions: WEO vs. World Bank's Global Economic Prospects (GEP): both project GDP, but GEP focuses more on developing countries and poverty
WEO vs. OECD Economic Outlook: OECD covers only its 38 members in depth; WEO is truly global
WEO vs. UN World Economic Situation and Prospects (WESP): UN report uses MER exclusively, leading to different global growth numbers
Critical trap: All four reports may show different global growth numbers for same year due to country coverage and weighting methodology differences

concepts.name: WEO's Role in IMF's Article IV Consultations and Surveillance Mandate
key_dimensions: WEO serves as the macro backdrop for IMF's bilateral surveillance (Article IV) of member countries
IMF's three-tier surveillance: bilateral (Article IV), regional (e.g., ASEAN, Euro Area), and multilateral (WEO)
WEO projections vs. Article IV Staff Reports: WEO is aggregated public document; Article IV reports are country-specific and sometimes confidential
How WEO findings can trigger IMF program negotiations or conditionality discussions with member countries

concepts.name: Concept of 'New Normal' and 'Secular Stagnation' in WEO Discourse
key_dimensions: WEO's adoption of 'New Normal' (post-2008) to describe structurally lower growth, lower inflation, lower interest rates in AEs
Alvin Hansen → Larry Summers 'Secular Stagnation' hypothesis as referenced in WEO analytical chapters
Post-2021 challenge to 'New Normal': inflation resurgence questioning whether low-rate era was temporary or structural
Implications for India: WEO's 'New Normal' debate affects global capital flows, FDI, and external demand for Indian exports

concepts.name: WEO on Debt in Emerging Markets: Sovereign Debt Crises and Restructuring
key_dimensions: WEO's monitoring of external debt, debt service ratios, and currency mismatches in EMDEs
WEO's coverage of 'Debt Distress' countries (especially LIDCs) — links to G20 Common Framework for debt restructuring
Distinction: WEO debt analysis vs. IMF's Debt Sustainability Analysis (DSA) — DSA is country-specific, WEO is aggregate
WEO on 'Original Sin' problem: EMDEs borrowing in foreign currency — vulnerability to exchange rate depreciation
